entries.topicDescription: Layered architecture patterns for Android: domain, data, and presentation boundaries.

tips.title: The domain layer should have zero Android framework dependencies
tips.content:
A domain module that imports android.* classes (Context, Bundle, even
androidx.lifecycle types) is much harder to test with fast, plain JVM unit
tests — Android classes aren't available there, so tests typically need
Robolectric or an instrumented device, slowing feedback loops significantly.

Keeping the domain module (use cases, business models, repository
interfaces) as pure Kotlin with no Android imports lets its entire test
suite run as fast, JVM-only unit tests — Android-specific concerns stay
confined to the data and presentation layers, which depend on domain, not
the other way around.

tips.title: A use case does one thing and is called like a function
tips.content:
A use case (interactor) wraps a single business action, such as GetUserProfile or PlaceOrder, so that logic lives in one named, testable class instead of being spread across ViewModels. Give it an operator invoke so the call site reads like a function call.

Keep use cases small and free of Android types. Not every screen needs one: a use case that only forwards a call to a repository adds indirection without value, so add one when there is real business logic to name or to share between screens.

tips.title: Map models at each layer boundary instead of sharing one class everywhere
tips.content:
If the same class is used as the network response, the database row and the UI state, a backend rename or a new column ripples through every layer. Give each layer its own model — a DTO for the network, an entity for the database, a domain model for business rules, and a UI model for the screen — and convert with small mapper functions at the boundary.

It costs a few lines of mapping code but keeps the domain layer stable and lets each layer change independently.

tips.title: Make the repository the single source of truth for offline-first data
tips.content:
Instead of letting the UI decide between network and cache, expose one Flow from the repository that always reads from the local database. Refreshing fetches from the network and writes into the database, and the Flow re-emits on its own.

The UI then has one data path, works offline by default, and never has to merge two sources. Handle refresh errors separately (a snackbar or a stale-data indicator) without clearing what is already shown.
